name: Periodic Table of Elements — Elements Lab
description: Structured data for all 118 known chemical elements, as presented in the Elements Lab interactive periodic table.

hasPart.name: Hydrogen
hasPart.description: Most abundant element in the universe; powers stars via fusion.

hasPart.name: Helium
hasPart.description: Second lightest element; makes your voice squeaky and balloons float.

hasPart.name: Lithium
hasPart.description: Lightest metal; core of modern rechargeable batteries.

hasPart.name: Beryllium
hasPart.description: Rigid, lightweight metal used in aerospace and X-ray windows.

hasPart.name: Boron
hasPart.description: Essential for plant growth; hardens glass and ceramics.

hasPart.name: Carbon
hasPart.description: Backbone of all known life; forms diamond and graphite.

hasPart.name: Nitrogen
hasPart.description: Makes up 78% of Earth's atmosphere.

hasPart.name: Oxygen
hasPart.description: Essential for respiration; makes up 21% of the air we breathe.

hasPart.name: Fluorine
hasPart.description: Most reactive element; added to toothpaste to fight decay.

hasPart.name: Neon
hasPart.description: Glows orange-red in the electric signs that bear its name.

hasPart.name: Sodium
hasPart.description: Reacts violently with water; essential for nerve function.

hasPart.name: Magnesium
hasPart.description: Burns with a brilliant white flame; vital in chlorophyll.

hasPart.name: Aluminium
hasPart.description: Lightweight, corrosion-resistant metal used in aircraft and cans.

hasPart.name: Silicon
hasPart.description: Foundation of computer chips and glass.

hasPart.name: Phosphorus
hasPart.description: Essential to DNA and ATP; glows faintly in the dark.

hasPart.name: Sulfur
hasPart.description: Smells of rotten eggs when combined with hydrogen.

hasPart.name: Chlorine
hasPart.description: Used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools.

hasPart.name: Argon
hasPart.description: Fills incandescent bulbs to stop the filament burning out.

hasPart.name: Potassium
hasPart.description: Critical for nerve signals and muscle contraction.

hasPart.name: Calcium
hasPart.description: Builds bones and teeth; fifth most abundant element in the body.

hasPart.name: Scandium
hasPart.description: Rare metal used in aerospace alloys and stadium floodlights.

hasPart.name: Titanium
hasPart.description: Strong as steel, half the weight; used in implants.

hasPart.name: Vanadium
hasPart.description: Strengthens steel; named after a Scandinavian goddess.

hasPart.name: Chromium
hasPart.description: Gives stainless steel its shine and corrosion resistance.

hasPart.name: Manganese
hasPart.description: Essential trace nutrient; hardens steel.

hasPart.name: Iron
hasPart.description: Core of Earth's magnetic field; most used metal on the planet.

hasPart.name: Cobalt
hasPart.description: Gives glass and ceramics a deep blue colour.

hasPart.name: Nickel
hasPart.description: Used in coins and rechargeable battery electrodes.

hasPart.name: Copper
hasPart.description: Excellent conductor; used in electrical wiring for millennia.

hasPart.name: Zinc
hasPart.description: Coats steel to prevent rust; essential trace nutrient.

hasPart.name: Gallium
hasPart.description: Melts in the palm of your hand at 30°C.

hasPart.name: Germanium
hasPart.description: Key semiconductor before silicon took over electronics.

hasPart.name: Arsenic
hasPart.description: Notorious poison; also used in semiconductors.

hasPart.name: Selenium
hasPart.description: Used in solar cells and to give glass a red tint.

hasPart.name: Bromine
hasPart.description: One of only two elements liquid at room temperature.

hasPart.name: Krypton
hasPart.description: Used in high-performance photographic flash lamps.

hasPart.name: Rubidium
hasPart.description: Highly reactive alkali metal used in atomic clocks.

hasPart.name: Strontium
hasPart.description: Gives fireworks their brilliant red colour.

hasPart.name: Yttrium
hasPart.description: Used in LED phosphors and superconductors.

hasPart.name: Zirconium
hasPart.description: Highly corrosion-resistant; used in nuclear reactor cladding.

hasPart.name: Niobium
hasPart.description: Superconducting metal used in MRI magnet wiring.

hasPart.name: Molybdenum
hasPart.description: Strengthens steel at high temperatures for jet engines.

hasPart.name: Technetium
hasPart.description: First artificially produced element; used in medical imaging.

hasPart.name: Ruthenium
hasPart.description: Hardens platinum and palladium alloys.

hasPart.name: Rhodium
hasPart.description: One of the rarest, most reflective metals; coats jewellery.

hasPart.name: Palladium
hasPart.description: Key catalyst in catalytic converters.

hasPart.name: Silver
hasPart.description: Best electrical conductor of any element.

hasPart.name: Cadmium
hasPart.description: Used in rechargeable nickel-cadmium batteries.

hasPart.name: Indium
hasPart.description: Coats touchscreens as a transparent conductor.

hasPart.name: Tin
hasPart.description: Prevents corrosion; alloyed into bronze since antiquity.

hasPart.name: Antimony
hasPart.description: Used since antiquity in cosmetics and alloys.

hasPart.name: Tellurium
hasPart.description: Alloyed into steel to improve machinability.

hasPart.name: Iodine
hasPart.description: Essential for thyroid hormone production.

hasPart.name: Xenon
hasPart.description: Powers ion thrusters on spacecraft.

hasPart.name: Caesium
hasPart.description: Defines the length of a second via its atomic clock.

hasPart.name: Barium
hasPart.description: Swallowed as a contrast agent for medical X-rays.

hasPart.name: Lanthanum
hasPart.description: Named the whole lanthanide series after itself.

hasPart.name: Cerium
hasPart.description: Most abundant rare-earth element; used in catalytic converters.

hasPart.name: Praseodymium
hasPart.description: Colours glass and ceramics a bright yellow-green.

hasPart.name: Neodymium
hasPart.description: Powers the strongest permanent magnets known.

hasPart.name: Promethium
hasPart.description: Only lanthanide with no stable isotopes; used in luminous paint.

hasPart.name: Samarium
hasPart.description: Used in high-temperature permanent magnets.

hasPart.name: Europium
hasPart.description: Provides the red phosphor in old CRT televisions.

hasPart.name: Gadolinium
hasPart.description: Used as a contrast agent in MRI scans.

hasPart.name: Terbium
hasPart.description: Green phosphor in energy-efficient lighting.

hasPart.name: Dysprosium
hasPart.description: Boosts the heat resistance of neodymium magnets.

hasPart.name: Holmium
hasPart.description: Has the highest magnetic strength of any element.

hasPart.name: Erbium
hasPart.description: Amplifies signals in fibre-optic communication cables.

hasPart.name: Thulium
hasPart.description: Rarest naturally occurring lanthanide.

hasPart.name: Ytterbium
hasPart.description: Used in atomic clocks more precise than caesium's.

hasPart.name: Lutetium
hasPart.description: Densest of the lanthanides; used in PET scan detectors.

hasPart.name: Hafnium
hasPart.description: Absorbs neutrons well; used in nuclear reactor control rods.

hasPart.name: Tantalum
hasPart.description: Highly corrosion-resistant; used in surgical implants and capacitors.

hasPart.name: Tungsten
hasPart.description: Highest melting point of any metal; lit old filament bulbs.

hasPart.name: Rhenium
hasPart.description: One of the rarest elements in Earth's crust.

hasPart.name: Osmium
hasPart.description: Densest naturally occurring element.

hasPart.name: Iridium
hasPart.description: A spike of it in rock layers marks the dinosaur extinction.

hasPart.name: Platinum
hasPart.description: Prized catalyst and jewellery metal, denser than gold.

hasPart.name: Gold
hasPart.description: Prized for millennia; never tarnishes.

hasPart.name: Mercury
hasPart.description: The only metal liquid at room temperature.

hasPart.name: Thallium
hasPart.description: Historically used as an odourless, tasteless poison.

hasPart.name: Lead
hasPart.description: Dense, soft metal once common in pipes and paint.

hasPart.name: Bismuth
hasPart.description: Forms colourful, iridescent crystals; least toxic heavy metal.

hasPart.name: Polonium
hasPart.description: Intensely radioactive; discovered by Marie Curie.

hasPart.name: Astatine
hasPart.description: Rarest naturally occurring element on Earth.

hasPart.name: Radon
hasPart.description: Radioactive gas that seeps from the ground into homes.

hasPart.name: Francium
hasPart.description: Among the rarest elements in Earth's crust; intensely radioactive.

hasPart.name: Radium
hasPart.description: Once used in glow-in-the-dark watch dials.

hasPart.name: Actinium
hasPart.description: Glows faintly blue in the dark from its own radioactivity.

hasPart.name: Thorium
hasPart.description: Proposed alternative nuclear fuel to uranium.

hasPart.name: Protactinium
hasPart.description: Rare and highly radioactive; found in trace amounts in uranium ore.

hasPart.name: Uranium
hasPart.description: Fuels nuclear reactors and weapons.

hasPart.name: Neptunium
hasPart.description: First transuranium element to be discovered.

hasPart.name: Plutonium
hasPart.description: Powered the Nagasaki bomb and Voyager spacecraft.

hasPart.name: Americium
hasPart.description: Used in household smoke detectors.

hasPart.name: Curium
hasPart.description: Used to analyse Martian soil on rover missions.

hasPart.name: Berkelium
hasPart.description: Named after Berkeley, California, where it was made.

hasPart.name: Californium
hasPart.description: Used to help start up nuclear reactors.

hasPart.name: Einsteinium
hasPart.description: Discovered in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test.

hasPart.name: Fermium
hasPart.description: Also discovered in hydrogen bomb test debris.

hasPart.name: Mendelevium
hasPart.description: First element made one atom at a time.

hasPart.name: Nobelium
hasPart.description: Named after Alfred Nobel.

hasPart.name: Lawrencium
hasPart.description: Named after physicist Ernest Lawrence.

hasPart.name: Rutherfordium
hasPart.description: Named after physicist Ernest Rutherford.

hasPart.name: Dubnium
hasPart.description: Named after Dubna, Russia, site of its discovery.

hasPart.name: Seaborgium
hasPart.description: Named after Nobel laureate Glenn Seaborg.

hasPart.name: Bohrium
hasPart.description: Named after physicist Niels Bohr.

hasPart.name: Hassium
hasPart.description: Named after the German state of Hesse.

hasPart.name: Meitnerium
hasPart.description: Named after physicist Lise Meitner.

hasPart.name: Darmstadtium
hasPart.description: Named after Darmstadt, Germany, where it was made.

hasPart.name: Roentgenium
hasPart.description: Named after physicist Wilhelm Röntgen.

hasPart.name: Copernicium
hasPart.description: Named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.

hasPart.name: Nihonium
hasPart.description: First element named by Japanese researchers.

hasPart.name: Flerovium
hasPart.description: Named after the Flerov Laboratory in Russia.

hasPart.name: Moscovium
hasPart.description: Named after Moscow, Russia.

hasPart.name: Livermorium
hasPart.description: Named after Livermore, California.

hasPart.name: Tennessine
hasPart.description: Named after the state of Tennessee, USA.

hasPart.name: Oganesson
hasPart.description: Heaviest confirmed element; named after physicist Yuri Oganessian.
